bib.title: Stochastic Linear Bandits with Sparsity (Chapter 23, Bandit Algorithms)
bib.venue: Bandit Algorithms, Cambridge University Press (book chapter, pp. 277-287)

question: How can a linear bandit learner avoid paying regret in the ambient dimension d when the parameter vector is sparse?
hypothesis: Regret should depend mainly on the sparsity m0 with only mild dependence on d.
contributions: Selective explore-then-commit (SETC) for the hypercube action set with regret O(||theta||_0 sqrt(n)) without knowing the sparsity
Online-to-confidence-set conversion giving a smaller ellipsoid and the OLR-UCB algorithm (Algorithm 14)
Sparse online linear predictor (Gerchinovitz) that yields regret O(sqrt(d n m0) log n), not computationally efficient

results.claim: SETC regret on the hypercube is instance-dependent and sums over nonzero coordinates only.
results.setup: Action set [-1,1]^d, ||theta||_1 <=1 style assumption (<theta,a> <=1), 1-subgaussian noise, horizon n known, sparsity unknown

results.claim: SETC minimax-style regret scales with the number of nonzero entries times sqrt(n log n), not d.
results.setup: Hypercube action set, same assumptions as Theorem 23.2; proof left as Exercise 23.2

results.claim: Linear UCB regret from Chapter 19 depends on d.
Hypercube worst-case lower bound without sparsity is linear in d.
results.setup: Hypercube, worst case over theta, shown in Chapter 24

results.claim: Sparse online linear regression regret is logarithmic in n.
results.setup: Online linear prediction under squared loss, theta with ||theta||_0<=m0 and ||theta||_2<=L, loglog terms dropped

results.claim: OLR-UCB with the sparse predictor has expected regret about sqrt(d n m0) times log factors (formula garbled in text extraction): O(sqrt(d n m0) log(n)^2) as read from the PDF; still depends on ambient d.
results.setup: General action sets, m0 known, Gerchinovitz predictor, rewards truncated w.h.p.

limits: The sparse online predictor behind Theorem 23.6 is not computationally efficient; no polynomial-time algorithm with logarithmic regret is known, so OLR-UCB has no efficient implementation (Note 1).
OLR-UCB needs the sparsity bound m0 and the norm bound m2 in advance; no algorithm achieves O(sqrt(||theta*||_0 d n)) for all sparsity levels at once (Note 4, Chapter 24).
The bound still depends on ambient dimension d, unavoidable in general (Theorem 24.3).
SETC needs the horizon n (not anytime, Exercise 23.3) and a hypercube action set.
Contextual sparse approaches with distributional assumptions (Kim and Paik 2019, Bastani and Bayati 2020) described as in their infancy.
No experiments, figures or code in this chapter; theory only.
practices: On a hypercube action set, explore each coordinate independently with Rademacher actions and commit once its confidence interval excludes 0: coordinates with theta_i=0 cost nothing (Sec 23.2).
Eliminate a coordinate from exploration (E=0) once 0 is outside its confidence interval; set A_ti = sign of the interval thereafter (Algorithm 13).
Confidence width W = 2 sqrt((1/T + 1/T^2) log(n sqrt(2T+1))) for T plays of coordinate i (Algorithm 13).
Convert any online linear regression regret bound B_t into an ellipsoid confidence set with radius beta_t(delta)=1+2B_t+32 log((sqrt8+sqrt(1+B_t))/delta) (Eq. 23.10, Theorem 23.4).
Use the tightest data-dependent online-learning regret bounds, since the gains can be significant (Note 3).
Passive-learning conditions (well-conditioned covariance) do not hold under a good bandit policy, since actions concentrate on the optimum (Sec 23.1).

terms.definition: ||theta||_0 = sum_i I{theta_i != 0}, the number of nonzero entries; not a true norm
The ratio of the largest and smallest eigenvalues of a positive definite matrix; well conditioned if small
Per-coordinate Rademacher exploration until the confidence interval excludes zero, then commit to the sign
Online prediction under squared loss with regret relative to a linear predictor theta
Online linear predictor UCB: optimistic action over a confidence set built from an online predictor's regret bound

code.snippet: Init E_1i=1, C_1i=R. Each t: B_ti~Rademacher; A_ti = B_ti if 0 in C_ti; 1 if C_ti subset (0,inf); -1 if C_ti subset (-inf,0). T_i(t)=sum_s E_si; theta_hat_ti = sum_s E_si A_si X_s / T_i(t); W_ti = 2 sqrt((1/T_i + 1/T_i^2) log(n sqrt(2T_i+1))); C_{t+1,i}=[theta_hat-W, theta_hat+W]; E_{t+1,i}=0 if 0 not in C_{t+1,i} or E_ti=0 else 1.

Each t: C_t={theta: ||theta||_2^2 + sum_{s<t}(Xhat_s - <theta,A_s>)^2 <= m2^2 + beta_t(delta)}; A_t = argmax_{a in A_t} max_{theta in C_t} <theta,a>; feed A_t to predictor, get Xhat_t; play A_t, observe X_t, feed X_t back.
